Q1: Does the paper provide a measure of robustness or risk? Answer 'Quantitative measure' if the paper defines or reports a numeric quantity it explicitly uses to characterize robustness or risk (e.g., maximum suboptimality, worst-case or tail error such as 99th-percentile or maximum q-error, variance of cost, share of regressed queries). Answer 'Qualitative measure' if robustness is assessed only by description or by visual inspection of results without such a quantity. Answer 'Mentioned but not measured' if robustness is claimed or discussed but neither assessed nor quantified. Answer 'Not provided' if robustness or risk is not discussed. Plain average performance metrics (mean runtime, mean q-error, speedup) alone do not count as a robustness measure. (Short Answers: Quantitative measure, Qualitative measure, Mentioned but not measured, Not provided)
Q2: Which part of the system does the paper's notion of robustness apply to? Consider the robustness the paper pursues or evaluates, whether it states a definition (new or existing) or only implies one, for example by aiming for robust plans, estimates or execution. Choose the label whose meaning best matches the part whose robustness is at stake; if several fit, choose the most specific one. Meanings: 'join ordering' = choosing the join order or join tree (e.g., a learned join-order selector); 'cardinality estimation' = estimating cardinalities or selectivities; 'cost model' = estimating the cost or runtime of plans or operators; 'plan optimization' = choosing among complete plans at optimization time (plan enumeration, plan selection, parametric or robust plan choice) when robustness is not tied to one of the parts above; 'workload management' = scheduling, admission control or resource allocation across queries; 'DBMS (end-to-end)' = query execution at run time (operators, adaptive or re-optimizing execution, fallbacks that avoid failures) or the system as a whole; 'ML models' = the robustness of learned models in general, when the paper does not tie it to one of the parts above. Answer 'No Definitions Provided' only if the paper neither defines robustness nor pursues it as a goal. Answer 'Unsure' if the part is ambiguous. (short answers: join ordering, cardinality estimation, cost model, plan optimization, workload management, DBMS (end-to-end), ML models, No Definitions Provided, Unsure)
Q3: Does the paper include formal theoretical content? Answer 'Yes' if it contains theorems, lemmas, propositions or proofs, or a formal analysis such as complexity bounds, approximation ratios or worst-case guarantees. Answer 'No' if it contains none of these; mathematical formulas that only define a model, a loss function or an evaluation metric do not count on their own. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. (Short answers: Yes, No, Unsure)
Q4: Does the paper include a significant experimental evaluation? Answer 'Yes' if it reports the results of experiments or simulations it ran, as tables or plots of measured outcomes (e.g., runtimes, estimation errors). Answer 'No' if it reports no measured results, e.g., a purely theoretical or analytical paper, or a demonstration paper that only describes demo scenarios; a single worked or illustrative example does not count as an evaluation. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. (Short answers: Yes, No, Unsure)
Q5: How does the paper evaluate the robustness of its approach or of the methods it studies? Answer 'experimental evaluation' if robustness is assessed through experiments or simulations with measured results. Answer 'theoretical evaluation' if robustness is assessed through formal analysis (proofs, bounds or guarantees). If both apply, give both labels separated by a semicolon. Answer 'Not provided' if the paper discusses robustness but does not evaluate it. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not address robustness. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. (Valid short answers: experimental evaluation, theoretical evaluation, Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q6: Is robustness a primary or a secondary contribution of the paper? Answer 'Primary' if robustness (e.g., to estimation errors, skew, drift, worst-case or tail behaviour) is the paper's main stated goal or a headline contribution, typically named in the title, abstract or list of contributions. Answer 'Secondary' if the paper's main goal is something else (e.g., accuracy, efficiency or speed) but it also claims, discusses or shows robustness benefits. Answer 'Not addressed' if robustness is not discussed. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. (Short answers: Primary, Secondary, Not addressed, Unsure)
Q7: What does the paper itself propose to improve robustness, and how does it achieve robustness? Classify the paper's robustness strategies using one or more of these options, the main one first, and include any additional techniques the paper adds on top of its main method (e.g., a fallback added to an adaptive executor): 'Run-time adaptation' = re-optimizes, switches plans or adapts during execution using statistics observed at run time; 'Worst-case guarantees' = bounds the worst-case suboptimality or error, often without relying on estimates; 'Risk-aware plan selection' = chooses plans by expected cost, variance, penalty or tolerance to estimation errors, not by a single point estimate; 'Uncertainty estimation' = the model quantifies the uncertainty of its own predictions; 'Robust operators' = operators that degrade gracefully under misestimation, memory pressure or skew; 'More accurate estimates' = better statistics, synopses or learned estimators that capture correlation and skew; 'Feedback-driven correction' = learns from executed queries to correct statistics, estimates or plans; 'Generalization and adaptation' = copes with drift or unseen databases or workloads through transfer, pre-training, domain adaptation or incremental updates; 'Regression safeguards' = guards against plans worse than the default, through fallback, validation models, guarded hints or consistency checks; 'Improved plan search' = a new or learned search strategy for plan generation; 'Robustness quantification only' = the paper measures or visualizes robustness but proposes no technique to improve it; 'Other' = a strategy not listed above. Then give the name of the paper's main proposed method as a whole, not only one of its components. Format: the options separated by semicolons, then ' — ' and the method name (e.g., 'Run-time adaptation; Regression safeguards — Adaptive query execution'). If the paper is an evaluation study, a survey, or a tool/demo that does not propose a new technique, or if no technique for robustness is proposed, answer 'Not provided'. A framework or methodology for evaluating or comparing methods is not a robustness technique. Do not name techniques from related work. (Valid short answers: Run-time adaptation, Worst-case guarantees, Risk-aware plan selection, Uncertainty estimation, Robust operators, More accurate estimates, Feedback-driven correction, Generalization and adaptation, Regression safeguards, Improved plan search, Robustness quantification only, Other, Not provided)
Q8: Which metrics or indicators does the paper use in its evaluation to assess robustness? List only measured quantities reported in the results (e.g., maximum or 99th-percentile q-error, maximum suboptimality, share of regressed queries, runtime under memory pressure). Do not list quantities that are part of the proposed method itself (e.g., a risk score used to select plans) unless they are also reported as evaluation results, and do not list mechanisms, logs or experimental parameters. If the paper reports only average performance (e.g., mean runtime, speedup, mean q-error) and does not assess robustness, list those metrics. If there is no evaluation, say 'Not provided'. The examples are illustrations, not a checklist: list only metrics that appear in the paper's results.
Q9: Which benchmarks, workloads or datasets are used in the paper's experimental evaluation? Use these canonical names exactly where they apply: JOB, CEB, STATS-CEB, Stack, DSB, TPC-H, TPC-DS, SSB, JCC-H, IMDb, DMV, Census, Forest, Power, Kddcup98, DBLP. Always write 'JOB' for the Join Order Benchmark and every variant of it: never write 'Join Order Benchmark', 'JOB-light', 'JOB-light-ranges', 'JOB-M' or 'JOB-Ext'. Name a benchmark workload rather than the dataset it runs on: when JOB is listed, do not also list IMDb. Name a dataset only when it is used without a named benchmark workload, e.g., DMV with generated queries. For anything not in the list, use the name the paper uses. For data the authors generate themselves, write 'synthetic'. Separate items with commas. Before answering, check every item and replace any name that has a canonical form with that form. Answer 'Not provided' if the paper reports experiments but does not name the data or workloads. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper reports no experiments. Answer 'Unsure' only if the description is ambiguous. (Valid short answers: [a list of the benchmarks, workloads or datasets used], Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q10: Is the data used in the experiments real, synthetic, or both? Classify the datasets (not the query workloads): data collected from real-world sources (e.g., IMDB, Stack, Forest, DMV, OpenStreetMap) is Real; data produced by a generator or benchmark data generator (e.g., TPC-H, TPC-DS, SSB, JCC-H, DSB, randomly generated tables) is Synthetic. Answer 'Both' only if the experiments use at least one real and at least one synthetic dataset. Generated queries over real data count as Real. Data produced in simulation studies counts as Synthetic. Answer 'Not provided' if the paper reports no experiments or does not say which data it uses. Answer 'Unsure' only if the description of the data is ambiguous. (Short answers: Real, Synthetic, Both, Not provided, Unsure)
Q11: Which characteristics of the data, queries or plans are deliberately controlled or varied in the experiments or in training-data generation (e.g., data skew, correlation, data size or scale factor, number of joins, predicate selectivity, query templates, workload drift)? List only such data, query or plan characteristics, and only those the paper's experiments actually vary; the examples are illustrations, not a checklist. Do not list hardware, software versions, model hyperparameters, training splits or method parameters. (Valid short answers: [a list of the characteristics controlled], Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q12: Does the paper include experiments explicitly designed to evaluate robustness, i.e., experiments that test behaviour under adverse or shifted conditions (e.g., injected estimation errors, skew, memory pressure, workload or data drift, unseen workloads) or that report worst-case, tail or regression behaviour as a robustness result? Ordinary performance comparisons on standard benchmarks do not count. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper reports no experiments. Answer 'No' if the paper reports experiments but none of them is designed to evaluate robustness (e.g., only ordinary performance comparisons on standard benchmarks). Answer 'Unsure' only if the experimental setup is ambiguous. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q13: Does the paper propose an approach that uses machine learning? Answer 'Yes' if the technique, model or system the paper itself proposes uses machine learning, including one that relies on a pre-trained model such as an LLM. Answer 'No' if the proposed approach does not use machine learning, or if the paper proposes no approach of its own. Methods the paper only evaluates or compares are not proposed by it. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. (Valid short answers: Yes, No, Unsure)
Q14: What type of machine learning does the proposed approach use? Answer 'Supervised' if models are trained on labelled examples (e.g., true cardinalities, costs or runtimes of training queries). Answer 'Unsupervised' if models learn from data without labels (e.g., a density model of the table data used for data-driven cardinality estimation). Answer 'Semi-supervised' if training combines labelled and unlabelled examples. Answer 'Reinforcement' if a policy learns from rewards by trial and error (e.g., execution feedback in join-order selection). Answer 'Other' for other learning paradigms (e.g., active learning, Bayesian optimization, or a pre-trained LLM used through prompting without training). If the approach combines several types, list each. Answer 'Not provided' if the paper uses machine learning but does not make the type clear. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. (Short answers: Supervised, Unsupervised, Semi-supervised, Reinforcement, Other, Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q15: What is the machine learning task of the proposed method? Answer 'Regression' if it predicts a numeric quantity (cardinality, cost, latency, or the parameters of a distribution over them). Answer 'Classification' if it predicts one of a fixed set of classes (e.g., which of two plans is faster, or which hint set to apply). Answer 'Learning-to-Rank' if it learns to order candidates (e.g., plans) by quality. Answer 'Autoregression' if it models a joint distribution as a product of conditional distributions (e.g., autoregressive data models for cardinality estimation). Answer 'Clustering' if it groups items (e.g., queries or plans) without labels. Answer 'Other' for other tasks (e.g., a reinforcement-learning policy that builds a plan step by step, or text generation by an LLM). If the method combines several, list each. Answer 'Not provided' if the paper uses machine learning but the task is unclear. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. (Valid short answers: Regression, Classification, Learning-to-Rank, Autoregression, Clustering, Other, Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q16: Does the proposed method use deep learning models? Answer 'Yes' if it uses a neural network (e.g., MLP, CNN, RNN, GNN, Transformer), including a pre-trained neural model such as an LLM or its embeddings. Answer 'No' if it uses only non-neural machine learning (e.g., tree ensembles, linear models, Gaussian processes, kernel density estimation, sum-product networks). Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q17: Does the proposed approach use transfer learning? Answer 'Yes' if it reuses a model pre-trained on other data or tasks, by fine-tuning, adapting (including domain adaptation) or applying it zero-shot to new databases or workloads; using a pre-trained LLM or embedding model counts. Answer 'No' if all models are trained from scratch on the target database or workload; retraining or incrementally updating a model on new data from the same database does not count. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q18: How is the training data of the proposed approach generated? List all that apply, separated by semicolons: 'Synthetic query generation' = random or template-instantiated queries generated over the database (including LLM-generated queries); 'Benchmark or production workload' = existing benchmark queries, query logs or historical executions; 'Execution feedback' = labels or experience obtained by executing plans (e.g., reinforcement-learning episodes, hint exploration, runtime measurements, telemetry); 'Optimizer-generated' = plans or traces produced by an existing optimizer or a simulator (e.g., expert demonstrations); 'Data sampling' = training on the table data itself (rows or samples), not on queries; 'Synthetic datasets' = generated databases or data distributions; 'Data augmentation' = generated or perturbed variants of existing training examples; 'Other' = another source. Answer 'Not provided' if the paper does not say how its training data is generated, or describes it only vaguely. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. (Valid short answers: Synthetic query generation, Benchmark or production workload, Execution feedback, Optimizer-generated, Data sampling, Synthetic datasets, Data augmentation, Other, Not provided, Not Applicable)
Q19: How are the inputs of the proposed model represented or encoded? List all that apply, separated by semicolons: 'Feature vectors' = flat vectors, one-hot encodings, bitmaps or histograms; 'Sets' = a set-based encoding of tables, joins and predicates (e.g., MSCN-style); 'Trees' = query plan trees; 'Graphs' = query or join graphs, or plan graphs; 'Sequences or text' = token or character sequences, SQL or plan text, or inputs to a language model; 'Data tuples' = the model takes table rows as input (e.g., data-driven estimators); 'Other' = another representation. Answer 'Not provided' if the paper does not describe the encoding. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. (Valid short answers: Feature vectors, Sets, Trees, Graphs, Sequences or text, Data tuples, Other, Not provided, Not Applicable)
Q20: Does the proposed approach handle predictive uncertainty? Answer 'Yes' if the method estimates the uncertainty of its own predictions (e.g., prediction intervals, variance, confidence scores, Bayesian or ensemble disagreement) or acts on it (e.g., falls back to a traditional optimizer, filters or reweights low-confidence predictions, chooses plans by risk). Answer 'No' if the paper only notes that estimates can be wrong, or reports prediction errors without estimating or using uncertainty. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q21: Does the study treat generalization to out-of-distribution inputs as a robustness concern, i.e., does it discuss performance on data, queries, workloads or databases that differ from those seen in training (e.g., unseen templates, workload drift, data updates, new databases)? Mentions only in related work do not count. Answer 'No' if the paper does not discuss this; use 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. (Valid short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q22: Does the study evaluate generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios, i.e., does any experiment test on data, queries, workloads or databases that differ from those used for training (e.g., held-out templates, unseen databases, drifted workloads, updated data)? Answer 'No' if no such experiment is reported; use 'Unsure' only if the experimental setup is ambiguous. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q23: Which model architecture does the proposed method use? Do not include architectures used only as a baseline. Meanings: 'MLP' = fully connected feed-forward layers; 'RNN' = recurrent networks over sequences, including LSTM and GRU; 'MSCN' = the multi-set convolutional network for sets of tables, joins and predicates; 'TCNN' = tree-convolutional networks over plan trees; 'Tree-LSTM' = LSTMs over plan trees; 'BDT' = tree ensembles or decision trees (e.g., gradient boosting such as XGBoost or LightGBM, random forests); 'GNN' = graph neural networks, including graph attention networks; 'Trm' = self-attention networks, Transformers and LLMs; 'Other' = any other model (e.g., Gaussian processes, sum-product networks, kernel density estimators, linear or Bayesian models). List several if the method combines them. Answer 'Not provided' if the paper uses machine learning but does not describe the model. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. Answer 'Unsure' only if the description is ambiguous. (Valid short answers: Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP), Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), Multi-set Convolutional Neural Network (MSCN), Tree-Convolutional Neural Network (TCNN), Tree-structured Long Short-Term Memory (Tree-LSTM), Boosted Decision Tree (BDT), Graph Neural Network (GNN), Transformer (Trm), Other, Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q24: Was improving robustness (e.g., to estimation errors, skew, worst-case or tail errors, drift or unseen workloads) a stated motivation for the design of the model or its input encoding? Answer 'Yes' if the paper states that a design choice of the model or encoding was made for such a reason, otherwise 'No'. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. Answer 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q25: Which of the following practices does the proposed approach use to make its learned models robust? List all that apply, separated by semicolons: 'Retraining or incremental adaptation' = updates the model as data or workload changes; 'Transfer or pre-training' = reuses a model trained on other databases or tasks; 'Data augmentation' = adds generated or perturbed training examples; 'Ensembles' = combines several models; 'Uncertainty or OOD detection' = detects unreliable predictions or inputs unlike the training data; 'Fallback or guard' = reverts to a traditional optimizer or a safe plan when the model may be wrong; 'Regularization' = constrains training, e.g., against overfitting or forgetting; 'Other' = another practice for model robustness. Do not list practices described only in related work, ablation studies, or future work. Answer 'Not provided' if none is used. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not propose an approach that uses machine learning. (Valid short answers: Retraining or incremental adaptation, Transfer or pre-training, Data augmentation, Ensembles, Uncertainty or OOD detection, Fallback or guard, Regularization, Other, Not provided, Not Applicable)
